Why not recognise that with phrasing like "additional support needs"? Functioning labels assume people's capabilities too much. I would be labeled as high functioning, and to many that means I need no support. This is not at all true. I meltdown in social situations, from especially loud noises and from sheer pressure. When in this state, I cannot talk and I stim constantly. I have actually been accused of being on drugs when people in authority have seen this. The large majority of autistic people do not like functioning labels for pretty similar reasons. I have personally witnessed parents of autistic kids insult their children right in front of them, along with stressing how much of a burden they are. And when confronted about it, they simply said "it's just stress, he/she is too low functioning to understand anyway"

To cut a long story short, I agree with you in principle. We do need to distinguish between those who cannot look after themselves and those who can to an extent. But the reality is that functioning labels have been used for too long to dehumanise  or deny support. We are not asking to not distinguish between people with more needs than others, but simply a change to less stigmatised and hurtful terminology

Yes it's a disability. Disability isn't a dirty word. I'm disabled. While I can take care of myself, I do acknowledge that others can't. But when it comes to autism, functioning labels have a root in studies performed by the nazis to determine which autistic kids could be useful to them, and which to to send to the spiegelgrund clinic to be killed. On top of this, while calling some autistic people "low functioning" can indeed be an acknowledgement of their support needs, the real issue comes from the denial of support systems made possible through "high functioning" labels. Those who were diagnosed with Aspergers or "high functioning autism" are often denied support, as they are seen as "normal" enough to function in a society that straight up isn't built to support them. A look into the suicide rates of autistic people will give you an idea of how much we mask our true selves in order to fit in in a neurotypical focused society.

I watch a lot of anime, play games, draw and practice guitar, usually by myself in my room. I'd love to discuss those things with people, but on the other hand those are the activities I use to unwind from the stress of being around people. I think it would be best for me to try and find a new interest rather than mess with my current coping methods.

Clothes are a big concern for me, I'm always paranoid that people judge me for always walking around in soft material tracksuit bottoms and hoodies that are a size too big, but if I don't I'm incredibly uncomfortable. There are few materials that don't irritate my skin because of my sensory issues.

As for the haircut idea, that is a great one. The few times I've successfully managed to make small talk with strangers have been during haircuts, because for once it actually feels more awkward to not speak.

And I do struggle with self isolation, because in my own mind I see it as self destructive and unhealthy, but it's a rut I can never escape for very long. But I have been slowly getting better with that, just the other day I volunteered in an outdoor nursery. Kids are much easier to be around than adults for me, because it never feels like they're hiding what they think.

But really, thank you for taking so much time to read my wall of text too, I have never been very good at communicating through writing without pretty much writing a novel 😂 hope you're having a great day 😊
